data.title: ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
data.description:
The bigger story for currency markets is the policy divergence. The RBA is now widely expected to start easing in mid-2027, while the Fed is still on a hiking path, with a December increase broadly expected. A narrowing rate gap between the two would weigh on the Australian dollar against the US dollar over time. Short-dated Australian rates may see limited reaction, because markets had already priced a June cut as more likely than not after the jobs data. The effect is more likely to show up further out on the curve. Any upside surprise in quarterly inflation would test ANZ's call quickly and could prompt a sharp repricing back toward a later start to easing.

---

data.title: Tokyo gets its first look at the Nvidia whiplash as Asia trades the Huang rebound
data.description:
Asian chip stocks get their first full chance today to respond to Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the setup differs sharply from market to market.

Tokyo is the clearest case. Japanese markets were shut on Monday for a public holiday, so today's session is the first since Friday's AI-led sell-off on Wall Street and Monday's sharp rebound, when the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%. Chip equipment and testing names with close ties to the AI supply chain, such as Advantest and Tokyo Electron, will be the ones to watch.

data.title: Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
data.description:
Goldman's framing favours the bottleneck parts of the AI supply chain, particularly memory makers, advanced packaging specialists and power infrastructure, over a single-stock bet on Nvidia. That is relevant for Asian equities, where memory and packaging exposure is concentrated in Korea and Taiwan. The view that neocloud lending now depends on milestones should ease some credit concerns around the sector, although it also implies slower, more conditional build-outs. The power angle ties AI spending to energy and utilities demand, a theme that is likely to keep electricity infrastructure in focus as data centre construction grows.

data.title: Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
data.description:
The Q&A softens the tone of Williams' prepared remarks without changing their core message, so pricing for a quarter-point hike on December 9 is unlikely to move much. His focus on unusual factors puts energy back at the centre. Brent is still around $92, well above the roughly $72 seen in late February before the US war with Iran began, so oil remains the main factor in how quickly 2027 delivers the lower inflation he expects. A sustained fall in crude would strengthen the case for a shallower hiking path next year, while fresh supply disruption would push the other way. His caution on hiring matters for the US dollar, since any slowdown in payrolls would weaken the case for further increases beyond December.

data.title: Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered.
data.description:
Asia gets the first real test today of whether the relief extends beyond US chipmakers: Tokyo reopens after a holiday, and Seoul's memory makers sold off before the news broke. In rates, a firmer equity backdrop gives the Fed cover to raise rates in December, which should keep short-dated Treasury yields supported and limit any pullback in the US dollar. Energy shares lagged during the rebound, which suggests the money returning to AI did not spill over into commodity-linked sectors. Nvidia volatility is likely to stay elevated into the December 1 congressional interview, since the stock now prices in a clean resolution of the security questions.

data.title: Jensen Huang is back in charge.  Nvidia moves higher.
data.description:
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had their best day since April 9, 2025, as buyers returned to beaten-down AI and chip stocks. Nvidia led the rebound, jumping $39.52 to $165.05 after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. The Nasdaq 100 gained 6.86%, the biggest move among the major US indices, while the Dow added more than 1,448 points.

The buying spread well beyond Nvidia. The Russell 2000 rose 3.40%, 26 of the 30 Dow stocks advanced, and S&P 500 gainers outnumbered decliners 406 to 79. Both Nasdaq indices recovered all of Friday’s losses, and the S&P 500 snapped a seven-session losing streak. data.title: Williams keeps December Fed hike in play as inflation seen above 2% until 2028
data.description:
Williams' remarks support pricing for a quarter-point hike in December and further tightening in 2027, which should keep front-end Treasury yields firm and give the US dollar some support. Energy features in his inflation story, and he calls the energy outlook uncertain, so any renewed rise in oil would add to the hawkish case. For equities, his message suggests the Fed will not step back from tightening just because stocks have been volatile, though the AI-led rally shows risk appetite can hold up under a hiking path. If December data come in hot, traders may start pricing a faster pace of increases next year.

data.title: Silver sets the technical boundaries in the short term for traders
data.description:
Silver is trading higher today after falling to its lowest level since September 2025 on Friday. The rebound took the price from $40.75 to a session high of $44.25, a gain of about 8.6% from Friday’s low. The move ran into sellers at the 100-hour moving average, however, and the price has since rotated lower.

The broader trend has been lower since September. Silver stalled at $67.30 on September 26 and moved back below its 100-day moving average, which was at $66.59 at the time. From there, the price stepped lower. The November 10 swing high at $53.72 marked the start of the latest leg down, which took silver to $40.75 on Friday.

data.title: Crude oil settles at $80.17. Trades at its lowest level since August 26.
data.description:
WTI crude oil fell nearly 4% Monday, trading near $80.20 a barrel around settlement after reaching an intraday low of $79.95. The selloff extends a slide that had already pushed crude to three straight weekly declines. So what gave sellers the upper hand today?

  • Libya’s Sharara pipeline reopened. Libya’s National Oil Corporation told Reuters that crude had begun flowing into storage tanks at Zawiya. The restart adds to supply availability at a time when traders are already watching for a surplus.
  • The market is looking ahead to more supply in 2027. The October rebound in Middle Eastern exports left more crude on tankers, and JPMorgan expects additional production from the Middle East outside Iran and from the Americas to contribute to a surplus next year. The bank sees oil futures in the high $70s in the first half of 2027.
  • A stronger dollar added a headwind. The dollar rallied alongside the Nvidia-led rebound in stocks. That makes dollar-priced crude more expensive for buyers using other currencies and added pressure to a market already selling off on supply news.

data.title: Gold rebounds 3.2% despite a stronger dollar and higher yields.
data.description:
Gold is up 3.2% today, trading near $3,654 after falling more than 9% last week and hitting its lowest level since September 2025. The rebound stands out with both the US dollar and Treasury yields moving higher. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest. So why is gold higher anyway?

The stock market rebound may be helping indirectly. As AI and chip stocks tumbled last week, some investors sold gold to raise cash and meet margin calls. With Nvidia leading a sharp rebound in equities today, some of that selling pressure may be easing. Gold was already recovering before the US stock market opened, suggesting dip buyers were stepping in early. I’d characterize the move as a relief rally after last week’s liquidation, with the improvement in risk sentiment helping it along.

data.title: Nvidia jumps 32.6% as AI and chip stocks rebound from last week’s rout. Nvidia is lifting all boats
data.description:
Nvidia is leading the rebound in AI and chip stocks after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO and board director. The shares were up 32.59% at $166.44 in Monday’s session, erasing last week’s 22.92% decline and trading 2.20% above their November 13 close. Western Digital and Coherent also recovered last week’s losses.

The buying is broad, but most names still have ground to make up. Nebius jumped 25.03% after falling 29.83% last week and was still 12.27% below its November 13 close. Sandisk gained 16.80% and remained 16.33% below that close, the largest remaining gap on the watchlist.
